questions.subtopic: SLA Dispute Escalates to Arbitration Mid-Recovery
questions.question: What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the chief financial officer?
questions.scenario_context: A retail bank ($6.8B in assets) has a critical core-banking vendor in active SLA breach (currently 78 hours into an outage). Mid-recovery (hour 50), the bank's general counsel informs the CFO that the vendor has formally invoked the contract's arbitration provision over a separate dispute (the vendor is alleging the bank withheld $4.2M in payments based on prior performance disputes). The arbitration filing was filed at 11pm Friday; the day before the current outage. Now the bank faces: (1) ongoing operational impact from current outage; (2) arbitration filing requires response within 30 days; (3) the vendor's posture suggests deteriorating relationship; (4) banking regulators monitoring the situation; (5) customer impact is escalating; (6) replacement vendor switching takes 6-9 months. The CFO is weighing strategy.

options.A: Pause arbitration response + focus on operational recovery + brief counsel for later + tag 30-day deadline + reassess after recovery + freeze vendor-comms + revisit settlement afterwards.
options.B: Settle arbitration immediately + accept vendor terms + structure payment plan + sign release + restore goodwill + accelerate recovery cooperation + close dispute.
options.C: Operational recovery + separate arbitration track under independent counsel + regulator engagement + documentation + alternative-vendor DD + executive briefing + customer notification.
options.D: Terminate contract for cause + cite outage as breach + serve termination notice + freeze payments + claim arbitration voided + emergency vendor switch + public statement.

questions.key_concept: SLA arbitration mid-recovery = operational recovery (priority) + separate arbitration response under independent counsel + operational/legal coordination + regulator engagement + documentation for both tracks + alternative vendor due diligence + executive briefing + customer/regulator notification. Eight tracks.
questions.pre_read: For SLA-arbitration-mid-recovery scenarios, anchor on "separate but coordinated operational + arbitration tracks under independent counsel." Pause-arbitration, settle-quickly, terminate-now framings each fail.
questions.correct_explanation: Federal Arbitration Act, AAA (American Arbitration Association) Commercial Rules, ISACA's IT Vendor Management Audit/Assurance Program, FFIEC Vendor Management Booklet, and corporate-litigation best practices establish eight-track response: (1) IMMEDIATE PRIORITY on OPERATIONAL RECOVERY; the current outage is the primary operational concern; (2) SEPARATE ARBITRATION RESPONSE TRACK under INDEPENDENT COUNSEL; operational and legal teams are separate; arbitration deadlines must be met regardless of operational situation; (3) OPERATIONAL/LEGAL COORDINATION; communications, decisions, document-management are separate channels but coordinated; (4) BANKING REGULATOR COORDINATION; supervisors monitor vendor disputes for banking-stability implications; (5) DOCUMENT EVERYTHING for BOTH operational recovery (the outage) AND arbitration evidence (prior performance disputes, payment-withholding context); (6) ALTERNATIVE-VENDOR DUE DILIGENCE; long-lead activity (6-9 months); not yet decision-time but option-preservation; (7) EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE + BOARD BRIEFING; operational + legal dimensions; (8) CUSTOMER COMMUNICATIONS + REGULATOR NOTIFICATION per contractual and supervisory expectations. Options A, B, D each represent strategic errors that compound the bank's exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Failure mode is pausing a parallel legal track during operational recovery. The vendor's filing the night before the outage may be designed to overwhelm response capacity; a paused arbitration risks default judgment at the 30-day deadline regardless of recovery progress, and the two tracks must run concurrently under independent counsel.
wrong_explanations.B: Failure mode is settling under maximum operational pressure without understanding the dispute substance. Payment plans, releases, and restored cooperation negotiated mid-outage produce bad terms, signal that aggressive vendor tactics succeed, and do not address the underlying operational and regulator issues.
wrong_explanations.D: Failure mode is declaring termination without the required contractual notice and opportunity-to-cure procedure. Termination notices, frozen payments, and emergency switches during an active outage layer additional litigation exposure on top of the existing arbitration; switching cost is 6-9 months.

tips: Trap is A: "pause arbitration response and focus on recovery" risks default judgment if 30-day deadline is missed; vendor's strategic timing may be designed to overwhelm bank's response capacity.

SLA arbitration mid-recovery = operational recovery + separate arbitration track + legal coordination + regulator + documentation + vendor due diligence + executive briefing + customer/regulator notification. Eight tracks.

Exam-day shortcut: any arbitration-during-vendor-crisis scenario is answered by SEPARATE COORDINATED TRACKS under independent counsel; pause-arbitration, settle-fast, terminate-immediate framings each fail.
questions.framework_ref: Federal Arbitration Act 9 USC §1; AAA (American Arbitration Association) Commercial Arbitration Rules; FFIEC Business Continuity Management Booklet; ISACA IT Vendor Management Audit/Assurance Program; Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (OCC/FRB/FDIC, 2023, superseding OCC Bulletin 2013-29)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SLA arbitration filed during vendor outage'. Public sources: FAA, AAA, FFIEC, ISACA. Scenario specifics (retail bank $6.8B, core-banking vendor 78-hour outage, arbitration filed previous Friday 11pm, $4.2M alleged withholding, 6-9 month replacement) invented.

questions.question: What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the chief audit executive at the conclusion of the year-long Operations & Resilience audit program?
questions.scenario_context: Following a comprehensive year-long audit of the firm's Operations & Resilience domain ($3.2B revenue financial services firm), the CAE is preparing to brief the audit committee. Findings: (1) IT operations maturity is moderately strong but with gaps in change governance and capacity planning; (2) cybersecurity operations have strong tools but underdeveloped threat-hunting; (3) BCP/DR is well-documented but exercise depth is insufficient; (4) cloud governance is fragmented across business units; (5) vendor management has solid controls for critical vendors but gaps for tier-2 vendors; (6) the firm faces upcoming regulatory examinations in 6 months. The CAE must structure the audit committee briefing.

options.A: Present each finding individually + management response per finding + risk rating per finding + regulatory-exam applicability notation + proposed remediation timeline.
options.B: Focus on the most severe findings + map each to upcoming regulatory exam requirements + provide management responses + recommend immediate remediation actions.
options.C: Present all findings with standardized risk ratings + categorize by domain + include management responses + note open vs. closed items + provide aggregate risk heat-map.
options.D: Cross-domain maturity + prioritized findings + remediation roadmap + regulatory exam alignment + management response + cross-functional dependencies + board governance + follow-up cycle.

questions.key_concept: Year-long Operations & Resilience audit conclusion = cross-domain maturity assessment + prioritized findings + remediation roadmap + regulatory exam alignment + management response framework + cross-functional dependencies + board governance recommendations + follow-up audit cycle + lessons learned. Nine tracks.
questions.pre_read: For year-long-audit-conclusion scenarios, anchor on "cross-domain maturity + prioritized roadmap + regulatory alignment + board governance recommendations." Finding-by-finding, severity-only, risk-rated-list framings each fail at the strategic level.
questions.correct_explanation: ISACA's Comprehensive Audit Methodology, IIA Standards on Internal Audit (especially Standard 2440 Disseminating Results), COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery) and MEA02 (Managed Internal Control), and audit-committee best practices establish nine-track briefing structure: (1) CROSS-DOMAIN MATURITY ASSESSMENT across IT ops, cyber, BCP/DR, cloud, vendor management; current state against industry benchmark using maturity model (e.g., COBIT 2019 5-level scale); (2) PRIORITIZED FINDINGS + REMEDIATION ROADMAP with timelines, owners, milestones; not a list but a structured plan; (3) REGULATORY EXAMINATION PREPARATION; 6-month horizon; alignment of findings with examiner focus areas; gives audit committee actionable prep view; (4) MANAGEMENT RESPONSE FRAMEWORK; agreed actions, escalation procedures, tracking metrics; not just acceptance/rejection but operational integration; (5) CROSS-FUNCTIONAL DEPENDENCIES; many findings span multiple domains (e.g., change governance gaps affect both IT ops and BCP/DR); cross-cutting view; (6) BOARD-LEVEL GOVERNANCE RECOMMENDATIONS; committee structure, reporting cadence (quarterly vs annual), oversight depth (operational vs strategic); (7) FOLLOW-UP AUDIT CYCLE STRUCTURE; when each area receives next audit; risk-based cycle; (8) LESSONS-LEARNED AND CONTINUOUS-IMPROVEMENT FRAMEWORK; what worked in this audit cycle, what to improve next cycle. Options A, B, C each represent tactical-level reporting that does not match the strategic audience.

wrong_explanations.A: A comprehensive finding-by-finding presentation with management responses, risk ratings, and remediation timelines looks rigorous and complete. The flaw is that presenting 60+ individual findings loses the cross-domain pattern that connects many of them (cloud fragmentation + vendor-management gaps + change-governance weaknesses are often expressions of the same underlying governance deficit). Audit committees operating at the strategic level need synthesized themes and prioritized roadmaps, not itemized inventories — the finding-by-finding format is appropriate for working-level remediation tracking, not board-level governance.
wrong_explanations.B: Severity-focused presentation mapped to regulatory exam requirements looks timely and strategically relevant given the 6-month examination window. The flaw is that limiting the briefing to the most severe findings omits the cross-domain pattern analysis that reveals compounding risk — moderate findings in multiple domains that share a root cause may collectively represent higher risk than the individual severity ratings suggest. Severity-only framing is reactive; audit committee briefings at this level require forward-looking strategic recommendations and board governance implications, not just a remediated list of top issues.
wrong_explanations.C: Standardized risk ratings organized by domain with a heat-map looks analytically disciplined and visually accessible. The flaw is that risk-rated lists and heat-maps are necessary documentation artifacts but insufficient for an executive-level briefing: they do not surface cross-functional dependencies (where one domain's finding blocks another's remediation), do not provide a strategic remediation roadmap sequenced against the regulatory examination timeline, and do not articulate board-governance implications. The format is operationally useful but strategically shallow for what the audit committee needs to fulfill its oversight mandate.

tips: Trap is A: "present each finding individually" creates 60+ items for audit committee review; loses cross-domain patterns, prevents prioritization discussion, and does not position the committee for strategic recommendations.

Year-long audit conclusion = cross-domain maturity + prioritized findings + remediation roadmap + regulatory alignment + management response + cross-functional dependencies + board governance + follow-up cycle + lessons learned. Nine tracks.

Exam-day shortcut: any year-long-audit-conclusion or capstone scenario is answered by STRATEGIC CROSS-DOMAIN view with maturity + roadmap + regulatory alignment; finding-by-finding, severity-only, list-format framings each fail.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Internal Audit Code of Ethics; IIA Standards on Internal Audit (2440 Disseminating Results, 2450 Overall Opinions); COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery), MEA02 (Managed Internal Control); ISO 19011 (Guidelines for Auditing Management Systems); ISACA IT Audit Standards on Reporting
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'D4 capstone — year-long Operations & Resilience audit conclusion'. Public sources: ISACA, IIA, COBIT, ISO. Scenario specifics (financial services $3.2B, year-long Operations & Resilience audit, multi-domain findings, 6-month examination horizon) invented.

questions.key_concept: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable elapsed time between a disruption and the restoration of a business process or IT service. RTO is measured in time and answers "how quickly must we be back online?"
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems; NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the Recovery Time Objective (RTO)?

options.A: The maximum acceptable elapsed time between a disruption and restoration of a business process or service.
options.B: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time prior to the disruption.
options.C: The total elapsed time required to return staff to full productivity after systems are restored.
options.D: The longest period an organization can survive without its critical systems before viability is threatened.

questions.correct_explanation: RTO is the target time within which a business process or IT service must be restored after a disruption to avoid unacceptable consequences. It is measured in elapsed time (minutes, hours, days) from the moment of disruption. ISO 22301:2019 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 both define RTO as a recovery objective focused on the duration of outage, not on data loss or downstream productivity. RTO drives the selection of recovery strategies such as hot/warm/cold site, replication, and standby capacity. Option B describes RPO. Option C describes WRT. Option D describes MTD.

wrong_explanations.B: This describes the Recovery Point Objective (RPO), which measures acceptable data loss in time (e.g., the last backup point), not the time required to restore service.
wrong_explanations.C: This describes Work Recovery Time (WRT) — the time after systems are restored that staff need to reconcile data, complete batch work, and return to full productivity.
wrong_explanations.D: This describes Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) — the outer ceiling beyond which the business itself is jeopardized. RTO must always be less than or equal to MTD.

tips: Mnemonic: RTO measures elapsed time the service is down — the T stands for Time-to-restore. Counted forward from outage start.
Disambiguation: RTO answers 'how fast back online?' RPO answers 'how much data can we lose?' MTD is the outer survival limit. WRT is the post-restore catch-up.
Exam shortcut: any answer about elapsed time to restore service = RTO. Any answer about data loss measured in time = RPO.
questions.pre_read: RTO = time to restore service after a disruption. Distinguish from RPO (data loss tolerance), WRT (post-restore catch-up), and MTD (outer survival limit).
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'RTO definition per ISO 22301:2019 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: ISO 22301:2019, NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1.

questions.key_concept: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time prior to a disruption. RPO answers "how much data can we afford to lose?" and drives backup frequency and replication strategy.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems; NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the Recovery Point Objective (RPO)?

options.A: The maximum elapsed time within which a service must be restored after disruption to avoid unacceptable consequences.
options.B: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time prior to a disruption.
options.C: The mean elapsed time between successive failures of a repairable system component.
options.D: The maximum total outage duration the business can survive before viability is threatened.

questions.correct_explanation: RPO is the target maximum age of files or data that must be recovered from backup storage for normal operations to resume. It is expressed in time (e.g., 15 minutes, 4 hours, 24 hours) measured backward from the moment of disruption. ISO 22301:2019 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 both define RPO as a data-loss tolerance objective that drives backup frequency, replication latency, and journaling strategy. An RPO of one hour requires backups or replication at least hourly. Option A describes RTO. Option C describes MTBF. Option D describes downtime cost, not RPO.

wrong_explanations.A: This describes the Recovery Time Objective (RTO), which measures elapsed time to restore service, not acceptable data loss.
wrong_explanations.C: This describes Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF), a reliability metric for repairable components, unrelated to backup recovery objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: This describes Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD), not RPO. MTD answers 'how long can we be down before the business fails?' — a downtime-tolerance metric. RPO answers 'how much data loss can we tolerate?' — a data-recency metric. Candidates conflate the two because both anchor BCP planning; MTD bounds RTO, while RPO bounds backup frequency.

tips: RPO = Recovery POINT Objective. The 'P' = Point in time to which data must be recovered. Measures acceptable data loss.
Disambiguation: RPO is BACKWARD in time (last good backup). RTO is FORWARD in time (how long until restored).
Exam shortcut: backup frequency drives RPO; recovery strategy drives RTO. Any question about acceptable data loss = RPO.
questions.pre_read: RPO = acceptable data loss measured in time. Drives backup and replication frequency. Distinguish from RTO (restoration time).
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'RPO definition per ISO 22301:2019 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: ISO 22301:2019, NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1.

questions.key_concept: A Business Impact Analysis (BIA) identifies critical business processes, quantifies the operational and financial impact of disruption over time, and establishes recovery objectives (RTO, RPO, MTD). The BIA is the foundational input to business continuity strategy.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 clause 8.2.2; NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.2; ISACA CISA Review Manual Domain 4
questions.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a Business Impact Analysis (BIA)?

options.A: To define the technical configuration of the recovery site and replication infrastructure.
options.B: To document the step-by-step procedures staff must follow when executing the disaster recovery plan.
options.C: To identify critical business processes and determine the impact of disruption over time.
options.D: To negotiate service level commitments with cloud and managed service providers.

questions.correct_explanation: The BIA is the analytical foundation of business continuity. Its primary purpose is to identify the organization's critical processes, quantify the operational, financial, regulatory, and reputational impact of their disruption over time, and use that analysis to establish recovery objectives (RTO, RPO, MTD) and process prioritization. ISO 22301:2019 clause 8.2.2 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.2 both place the BIA before strategy selection. The BIA's outputs feed the BCP/DRP, not the other way around. Option A is a strategy/design activity that follows BIA. Option B describes DRP procedures. Option D describes SLA negotiation.

wrong_explanations.A: Designing the recovery site is part of the recovery strategy phase, which uses BIA outputs (RTO/RPO) as inputs. It is a downstream activity, not the purpose of the BIA.
wrong_explanations.B: Step-by-step recovery procedures are documented in the Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP), produced after the BIA has set objectives and after strategies have been selected.
wrong_explanations.D: Negotiating SLAs is a sourcing and contractual activity. While BIA outputs may inform SLA targets, SLA negotiation itself is not the purpose of the BIA.

tips: BIA = Business IMPACT Analysis. The whole point is to quantify IMPACT of disruption over time.
Disambiguation: BIA identifies WHAT is critical and HOW MUCH disruption costs. The BCP/DRP then describes WHAT TO DO about it.
Exam shortcut: BIA always precedes strategy selection. RTO/RPO/MTD are OUTPUTS of the BIA, not inputs.
questions.pre_read: BIA identifies critical processes, quantifies impact over time, and sets RTO/RPO/MTD. It precedes BCP/DRP strategy selection.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'BIA primary purpose per ISO 22301:2019 and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: ISO 22301:2019 clause 8.2.2, NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.2.

questions.key_concept: A hot site is a fully equipped alternate facility with hardware, software, network, and current data replication that can take over operations within hours. A warm site has hardware and infrastructure but requires data restoration. A cold site provides space and utilities only.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.4.2 Alternate Sites; ISACA CISA Review Manual Domain 4
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes a hot site?

options.A: A facility with hardware and network infrastructure but no current data, requiring restoration from backups.
options.B: A facility providing physical space, power, and environmental controls but no installed IT equipment.
options.C: A reciprocal arrangement with another organization to share computing facilities during a disruption.
options.D: A fully equipped facility with hardware, software, and current data ready for rapid cutover within hours.

questions.correct_explanation: A hot site is the most expensive and fastest-to-activate alternate site option. Per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.4.2, it is a fully operational facility with hardware, system software, applications, network connectivity, and current or near-current data (via replication or frequent restoration). Recovery times are typically measured in hours, supporting low-RTO requirements. Option A describes a warm site. Option B describes a cold site. Option C describes a reciprocal agreement, which is a separate alternate-site option.

wrong_explanations.A: This describes a warm site — hardware and infrastructure are in place but data is not current, so recovery requires loading recent backups before cutover. Recovery is faster than a cold site but slower than a hot site.
wrong_explanations.B: This describes a cold site — space, power, and HVAC only. Hardware must be procured or moved in and software installed before recovery can begin, taking days to weeks.
wrong_explanations.C: This describes a reciprocal (mutual aid) agreement, a separate alternate-site arrangement. While useful, it is not the definition of a hot site.

tips: Hot = HOT and ready (data current, fastest, most expensive). Warm = warming up (hardware ready, data must load). Cold = empty room (space only, slowest, cheapest).
Disambiguation: the temperature maps to readiness. Hotter = closer to running. Colder = more work needed before recovery.
Exam shortcut: any answer mentioning current data and rapid cutover = hot site. Empty space with utilities = cold site.
questions.pre_read: Hot site = fully equipped, data current, hours to recover. Warm = hardware only. Cold = space and utilities only.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hot/warm/cold site definitions per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.4.2, ISACA CISA Review Manual.

questions.key_concept: ITIL 4 defines Incident Management as the practice of minimizing the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible. The goal is restoration of service, not root-cause determination, which belongs to Problem Management.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Foundation, Incident Management practice
questions.question: What is the PRIMARY goal of the ITIL 4 Incident Management practice?

options.A: To restore normal service operation as quickly as possible and minimize business impact.
options.B: To identify the underlying root cause of recurring failures and eliminate it permanently.
options.C: To assess, authorize, and schedule changes to IT services with minimal disruption.
options.D: To define service level targets and report on achieved performance to customers.

questions.correct_explanation: Per ITIL 4, Incident Management is the practice of minimizing the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible. The emphasis is on speed of restoration — a workaround that brings the service back is acceptable even if the underlying cause is not yet known. Root-cause analysis is explicitly the responsibility of Problem Management, which operates on a longer time horizon. Option A captures the speed-of-restoration goal. Option B describes Problem Management. Option C describes Change Enablement (Change Management). Option D describes Service Level Management.

wrong_explanations.B: Root-cause elimination is the goal of Problem Management, not Incident Management. The two practices are deliberately separated so service restoration is not delayed by root-cause investigation.
wrong_explanations.C: Assessing and scheduling changes is the goal of Change Enablement (called Change Management in earlier ITIL versions), a distinct practice from Incident Management.
wrong_explanations.D: Setting and reporting on service targets is Service Level Management. It interacts with Incident Management (incidents may breach SLAs) but is a separate practice with a different goal.

tips: Incident Management's job is speed of restoration: get the service back fast, even with a workaround. Root-cause work waits for Problem Management.
Disambiguation: Incident Management restores service. Problem Management finds and fixes root cause. They are deliberately separate.
Exam shortcut: 'restore service as quickly as possible' = Incident Management. 'eliminate root cause' = Problem Management.
questions.pre_read: ITIL 4 Incident Management = restore normal service as quickly as possible. Root cause is Problem Management's job.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ITIL 4 Incident Management goal and definition'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: ITIL 4 Foundation publication.

questions.key_concept: RAID 1 (mirroring) writes identical data to two or more disks, providing full redundancy and fast read performance at the cost of 50 percent usable capacity. It tolerates the loss of any one disk in a mirrored pair without data loss.
questions.framework_ref: Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA) Common RAID Disk Data Format Specification; ISACA CISA Review Manual Domain 4
questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing storage controls confirms a database server uses RAID 1. Which BEST describes the protection RAID 1 provides?

options.A: Data is striped across multiple disks with no redundancy, providing performance but no fault tolerance.
options.B: Data is striped across disks with distributed parity, tolerating a single disk failure across the set.
options.C: Identical data is written to two or more disks, providing mirroring and tolerance of a single disk failure.
options.D: Data is striped across disks with double distributed parity, tolerating two simultaneous disk failures.

questions.correct_explanation: RAID 1 is the mirroring configuration: every block written to one disk is written identically to one or more mirror disks. It provides full redundancy — the loss of any one disk in a mirrored pair causes no data loss because an identical copy remains. Usable capacity is half (or less) of raw capacity. Read performance benefits because reads can be served by either disk. Option C is the correct mirroring definition. Option A describes RAID 0 (striping, no redundancy). Option B describes RAID 5 (striping with single parity). Option D describes RAID 6 (striping with double parity).

wrong_explanations.A: This describes RAID 0, which stripes data for performance but provides no redundancy. Loss of any disk in a RAID 0 set destroys the entire array's data.
wrong_explanations.B: This describes RAID 5, which stripes data with a single parity block distributed across all disks. It tolerates one disk failure but is not mirroring.
wrong_explanations.D: This describes RAID 6, which uses two independent parity calculations distributed across disks. It tolerates two simultaneous disk failures but is not mirroring.

tips: RAID 1 = mirror = 1 copy on each disk. Half the capacity, full redundancy, simplest fault tolerance.
Disambiguation: RAID 0 = stripe only (no protection). RAID 1 = mirror. RAID 5 = stripe + 1 parity. RAID 6 = stripe + 2 parity. RAID 10 = mirror + stripe.
Exam shortcut: any answer mentioning 'identical copies' or 'mirroring' = RAID 1. Parity-based answers = RAID 5 or 6.
questions.pre_read: RAID 1 = mirroring. RAID 0 = striping only. RAID 5 = striping with one parity. RAID 6 = striping with two parities. RAID 10 = mirror + stripe.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'RAID 1 mirroring definition'. Foundational recall tier. Public sources: SNIA Common RAID DDF, ISACA CISA Review Manual.
